page_title: Why bother writing tests at all?

sources.entry: Why bother writing tests at all?, Dave Cheney. A good intro to the topic.

summary.title: Why bother writing tests at all?
summary.one_liner: Dave Cheney argues that development teams should write most of the automated (mostly unit) tests, because manual testing doesn't scale, tests keep master shippable, and tests lock in behaviour and let future maintainers change code safely.
takeaways: Most testing should be automated and done mainly by development teams, with unit tests as the bulk.
Manual testing does not scale; it is expensive, boring and tends to get skipped as the number of tests grows.
Write a failing automated test before fixing a bug or adding a feature, then check in the test with the fix.
Keep the master branch always shippable; tests passing is the gate for that.
Tests act as an executable contract for behaviour and give confidence to change code written by others.
summary.summary: The post is the concluding piece of a series on testing, asking why software should be tested at all and who should do the testing. Cheney argues that development teams should write the majority of automated tests, mostly unit tests, while still allowing integration, end-to-end and QA roles. He contrasts this with manual testing, which he says does not scale. The essay then covers how tests keep the master branch shippable, lock in behaviour as a contract, and help future maintainers change code safely.
